content.text: I'll file this as an inconclusive investigation, since that is what the record supports.

assumptions: That the alert itself was accurate is assumed, not verified — with no metrics retrieved, we have no independent confirmation that the error rate was actually elevated, and a false alert has not been ruled out.
Customer impact is unknown in both directions. No impact was measured, and the absence of a measurement is not evidence that impact was zero.
The incident is assumed to be unresolved. Nothing in the record shows a fix, a rollback, or a return to healthy behaviour, so the condition may still be present.

The cause of the empty metrics read is assumed to be unknown. Whether it was a bad query, a missing service, or a metrics-platform failure was never established, and the distinction matters for how much other alerting is affected.
The sub-second start-to-end span is assumed to describe the automated handling rather than the duration of any real degradation.
input.executive_summary:
An automated alert fired reporting an elevated error rate on one of our backend services. The automated responder picked the alert up, attempted to pull the service's recent performance data for the minutes around the alert, and got nothing back — the data it needed to confirm or characterise the problem was unavailable. With no evidence to work from, it handed the incident off to humans immediately rather than guessing.

As a result we cannot say from this record whether customers were affected, how many requests failed, or how long any degradation lasted. No changes were made to the service, no remediation was attempted, and nothing was confirmed to be fixed. The alert's own start and end timestamps are less than a second apart, which reflects how quickly the automated handling opened and closed out its part of the work; it should not be read as a measurement of how long the underlying problem lasted.

The actionable finding is about our tooling rather than the service: the metrics read returned zero data points, and until that is explained, alerts on this service cannot be triaged automatically. Follow-ups should be (1) determine why the metrics query came back empty — wrong time window, wrong service identifier, or a metrics pipeline outage — and (2) re-examine the service's error rate for the affected period from a source that does return data, to establish whether there was a real customer-facing failure here.
input.root_cause: Undetermined. The only diagnostic step taken was a request for the service's per-minute metrics anchored on 14:03, which returned no data points, so the investigation produced no evidence about what drove the error rate; the incident was escalated in the same second it was opened. The one "candidate cause" on the record is a placeholder stating that no metrics were retrieved, not a hypothesis about the service, and it was never tested.
